Testimony of Rep. Allison Hepler presenting

LD 1561, Resolve, Regarding the Percentage of a Lobster and Crab

Fishing Licensee's Lobster Traps That May Be Fished in a Lobster

Management Zone Listed on the License as a Secondary Zone

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Marine Resources

Good afternoon, Senator Tepler and colleagues on the Marine Resources Committee. I am Allison Hepler and I represent the towns of Arrowsic, Georgetown, Phippsburg, West Bath and Woolwich. I am
here today to present LD 1561, Resolve, Regarding the Percentage of a Lobster and Crab Fishing
Licensee's Lobster Traps That May Be Fished in a Lobster Management Zone Listed on the
License as a Secondary Zone.

This bill had its genesis in a conversation I had last fall with several lobstermen who fish in Zone E and their concerns about the number of lobstermen who had secondary trap tags allowing them to place their traps in Zone E. Currently, Maine statute allows fishermen to place up to 49% of their gear in "other
zones," commonly called "secondary zones," as long as they indicate these declarations on their license.
Zone E adopted a 600-trap limit in 2000 for conservation reasons. Having up to 49% of traps from fishermen in other zones being fished in Zone E can limit the impact of that conservation effort. This
prompted a long conversation about various ways the zones could maintain some level of control over
the number of traps fished in any particular zone. We also speculated on any unintended consequences
and whether each zone council would have the authority (or want to have the authority) to limit
secondary tags. We also discussed whether changing the percentage of secondary tags or changing it to a specific number of tags would work. We wondered whether the concerns were more prevalent for
fishermen who fish on the zone line.

This resolve is the result of those conversations. And it coincides with this committee's desire for more
involvement in zone councils and promoting more decision making within zone council authority. This resolve asks the Department of Marine Resources to seek feedback from the zone councils about this issue and to come back to this committee with results and any recommendation regarding secondary traps. I chose a resolve in order to preserve the option of submitting a bill in the Second Regular Session of the 132"" Legislature based on the report from the Department.

Thanks for youri time and I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

TESTIMONY OF
Deirdre Gilbert
Department of Marine Resources

The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying

In Support of

-

LD 1561 Resolve, Regarding the Percentage of a Lobster and Crab Fishing Licensee's Lobster Traps

That May Be Fished in a Lobster Management Zone Listed on the License as a Secondary Zone

Before the Committee on Marine Resources

Sponsored by Representative Hepler

Date of Hearing: April 17, 2025

Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine
Resources, my name is Deirdre Gilbert, Director of State Marine Policy for DMR and l am testifying on
behalf of the Department in support of LD 1561.

Under current law, when a lobster license holder purchases their license, they must designate their primary Zone, where they fish a majority of their traps, as well as any secondary Zones, where they might fish any of their gear, not to exceed 49%. When Zones were originally established, the Zone lines were for voting purposes only, and did not limit where someone could fish. However, with the establishment of limited entry, it became necessary to require that license holders fish the majority of their gear in their "home" Zone. The opportunity to identify secondary zones was created to accommodate individuals who live along the Zone lines to provide a reasonable level of fishing across
Zone lines.

Since that time, there have been periods where conflicts have flared up, due to situations where one Zone appears to be bringing more gear into its neighboring Zone than vice versa. Currently, the Department is aware that there has been that concern from Zone E --- specifically, that Zone F fishermen are bringing more gear, and further, into Zone E than has historically been the case, negatively impacting Zone E fishermen. Zone E and Zone F have recently created subcommittees working together on this topic which has met once, with another meeting currently planned for May.
This is a challenging problem to solve, but DMR would be happy to bring this issue to each Zone
Council to see if there is any consensus for changing the percentage of gear that may be fished outside
of a license holder's home Zone. We will bring that information back to this committee with any
recommendations that may result.

Thank you for your consideration and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
10044914:
Ethan DeBery Phippsburg LD 1561
The lobster fishery needs another mechanism to address folks from fishing beyond their home zone. I fish in zone E where the trap limit has been voted down to 600 traps for conservation and to reduce congestion. Essentially, we took a few cattle out of our field let our grass grow taller and give our cows a little more space. Now our neighbor take a look at our field and say that looks pretty nice and then put half their cows onto our field. Something's needs to be done to dial this back. Zone lines are imaginary lines in the ocean and are not perfect boundaries of fishing grounds so some overlap is necessary. But fishing half your gear in someone else's pasture is a little much. Maybe folks can still fish half their gear outside their home zone but only a quarter in any other particular zone.
All I know is folks from other zones with higher trap limits fishing in our zone are seriously undermining our conservation effort going from 800 to 600 traps. We need another tool to address this issue and there is nothing in the current legal/regulatory framework to work with.
10044880:
Dear Honorable Members of the Marine Resources Committee:
I am writing to support LD 1561: Resolve, Regarding the Percentage of a Lobster and Crab Fishing Licensee's Lobster Traps That May Be Fished in a Lobster Management Zone Listed on the License as a Secondary Zone.
This issue is important to those who fish on the western side of Zone E in the traditional waters surrounding Small Point. Over the years, we have seen a steady trend of more and more vessels fishing in zone E, creating crowding issues and uncertainty over the distribution of landings and the effect upon the communities dependent upon the lobster resource.
From 2016 to 2024 Zone E saw 21 additional fishermen from Zone F fishing Zone E waters, resulting in the potential addition of 6,174 traps being fished in these waters. This creates the effect of transferring landings from one community to another, adversely impacting vessels, captains, crew, buying stations and the extended community. It is also a trend that appears to have no end in sight.
Zone E had voted early on in the zone process to a lower 600 trap limit due to density issues within Zone E. Zone E is one if not the smallest zone by area. The addition of all this new effort has negated and rolled back any benefits from Zone E voluntarily lowering its trap limit.
The amount of gear going from one zone to another also raises issues with the limited entry system. Each zone creates its ratios it deems fit for balancing the amount of effort to let into that particular zone. If another zone is allowed to flood into another, it is essentially a back door around the exit to entry ratios.
This is one step we hope in a process to provide some stability and relief long term for those negatively impacted by this effort redistribution.
Lawrence Pye Small Point Harbor
10044974:
In Support of
LD 1561 Resolve, Regarding the Percentage of a Lobster and Crab Fishing Licensee's Lobster Traps That May Be Fished in a Lobster
Management Zone Listed on the License as a Secondary Zone
April 17, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Marine Resources Committee, the Maine Lobstermen's Association (MLA) submits this testimony in support of LD 1561 to direct Maine Department of Marine Resources to solicit feedback from the lobster zone councils regarding the proportion of lobster traps that may be fished in a secondary zone.
The MLA is a strong supporter of Maine's zone council process which has been in place since the late 1990's. The zone councils were established to give lobstermen a voice in the management of their local fishing areas, recognizing the diversity of Maine's lobster fishery along the coast. The system works because lobstermen elect their local zone council members and are invested in ensuring the sustainability of the both the lobster resource and their local fishery.
The regulations requiring lobstermen to fish the majority of traps in their home zone, and to tag traps fished in secondary zones, ensure that lobstermen maintain control of their local areas. For the zone council system to work, the majority of gear fished in a zone must be fished by local fishermen. They must not be at risk of being crowded out or outnumbered by lobstermen from other zones. This is very important because lobster abundance has increased significantly, first in the mid-coast Maine region and then Downeast. The zone council system prevents lobstermen from targeting lobster hotspots with all of their gear, limiting the amount of fishing pressure in areas where the stock is most productive. It has become an important conservation tool.
The Gulf of Maine, the lobster resource, and the fishery itself have experienced significant changes since the zone council system was first implemented. Zone Councils have served the industry well, but it is important to re-evaluate elements of the system to ensure that it continues to support the present-day, and future, Maine lobster fishery. These conversations should start with the zone councils.
The MLA urges you to support LD 1561. Thank you for your consideration.
